items.description: Ensure their Go concurrent code follows battle-tested patterns that prevent goroutine leaks, timer churn, and channel misuse.
items.summary: The golang-concurrency skill v1.1.4 from samber cc-skills-golang teaches structured concurrency where every goroutine has a clear owner, exit path, and error propagation. Write mode implements goroutines, channels, sync primitives, worker pools, and pipelines. Review mode inspects PR diffs for leaks, missing context propagation, ownership violations, and unprotected shared state. Audit mode parallelizes up to five sub-agents to find spawns without shutdown, unsynchronized globals, channel misuse, hot-loop time.After calls, and mutex problems. Core principles require sender-only channel closes, unbuffered channels by default, ctx.Done in select, and goleak in tests. Tables compare channels versus mutexes versus atomics and WaitGroup versus errgroup with SetLimit for bounded workers. Reference docs cover channels and select, sync primitives, and fan-out fan-in pipelines. Common mistakes include fire-and-forget goroutines, receiver-side channel closes, wg.Add inside goroutines, and mutexes held across I/O.
highlights: Structured concurrency rules: every goroutine needs a clear exit, owner, and error propagation path.
Write, review, and audit modes with up to five parallel sub-agents for large codebase concurrency scans.
Channel versus mutex versus atomic decision tables plus WaitGroup versus errgroup guidance.

items.name: golang-context
items.author: samber
items.description: Ensure AI coding agents produce correct Go context propagation and cancellation patterns in HTTP handlers and concurrent code.
items.summary: The golang-context skill v1.2.1 teaches idiomatic context.Context usage as the request session tying together handler, service, database, and external API work. Eleven best-practice rules require ctx as the first parameter, prohibit storing context in structs, mandate cancel on all WithCancel paths, restrict context.Background to top-level entry points, and limit values to request-scoped metadata with unexported key types. Creating contexts table maps Background, TODO, r.Context, WithCancel, and WithTimeout to appropriate situations. Propagation examples contrast breaking the chain with context.Background inside services versus passing caller ctx to db.ExecContext. Deep-dive references cover cancellation and WithoutCancel for audit logs that outlive requests, safe value keys for tracing, and HTTP client plus QueryContext database patterns. Cross-references link to golang-concurrency, golang-database, golang-observability, and golang-design-patterns skills. Linters like govet and staticcheck catch many context pitfalls automatically during review.
highlights: Eleven must-follow rules for ctx first parameter, no struct storage, and cancel on all control paths.
Propagation principle: same context flows handler to service to database to external APIs.
Documents WithCancel, WithTimeout, WithDeadline, and Go 1.21+ WithoutCancel for outliving work.
Context values limited to request metadata with unexported keys, never function parameters.
HTTP and database sections require r.Context, NewRequestWithContext, and QueryContext variants.

items.name: golang-data-structures
items.author: samber
items.description: Select, explain, and optimize the right data structures for performance-critical code.
items.summary: The golang-data-structures skill v1.1.3 helps Go engineers pick structures by memory layout, allocation cost, and access patterns rather than familiarity alone. Eight summary rules recommend preallocating slices and maps with known capacity, preferring arrays only for fixed compile-time sizes, using container/heap for priority queues, the strings package for string assembly, bytes.Buffer for bidirectional I/O, tightest generic constraints, and weak.Pointer caches in Go 1.24+. Slice internals explain three-word headers, capacity growth doubling below 256 elements then roughly twenty-five percent, and slices.Grow pre-expansion. Map sections cover hash buckets, make with size hints, and Go 1.21+ maps package helpers like Clone and Equal. Container packages, generic collections, pointer semantics, and copy-versus-reference guidance link to golang-safety and golang-concurrency for aliasing and channel topics. Reference files provide slice and map deep dives plus container selection tables for everyday service code.
highlights: Eight best-practice rules for preallocation, container choice, string assembly versus Buffer, and weak.Pointer caches.
Slice internals cover header layout, growth algorithm, and slices package Sort, BinarySearch, Grow helpers.
Map guidance includes bucket structure, make size hints, and maps package Clone and Equal functions.
Compares container/heap, list, and ring for priority queues, middle inserts, and circular buffers.
Documents unsafe.Pointer six valid conversion patterns and Go 1.24+ weak.Pointer for GC-friendly cache maps.

The skill includes diagnostic loops to identify which value lever is broken, reference guides on guarantee design and bonus stacking, and format playbooks tailored by business type.
highlights: Value equation framework: optimize dream outcome, perceived likelihood, time delay, and effort/sacrifice to increase per
Six-component offer anatomy checklist: core deliverable, bonus stack, guarantee, scarcity/urgency, name, price and payme
Diagnostic loop to identify binding constraint: score each value lever 1-10, audit missing components, fix one lever per
Reference guides for guarantee design, bonus stacking, scarcity patterns, and format playbooks (service, course, coachin
Guidance on what NOT to do: fake scarcity, over-promising guarantees, bonus inflation, and pattern-matching scam languag

items.name: golang-samber-slog
items.author: samber
items.description: Ensure Claude, Cursor or Codex correctly composes a production-grade slog logging pipeline in Go using the samber/slog ecosystem.
items.summary: samber/slog-**** is a collection of 20+ composable slog.Handler packages for Go 1.21+ implementing a canonical logging pipeline. Developers use it to build production logging architectures where records flow through sampling (to reduce noise), formatters (to strip PII), and routers (to send errors to Sentry while info goes to Loki). It matters because sampling before formatting saves CPU, and routing separates concerns without duplicating handlers.
highlights: 20+ composable handler packages for structured logging
Canonical pipeline: sampling - formatting - routing - sinks
Integrates with Datadog, Sentry, Loki, and 15+ backends

items.description: Ensure their Go services produce clean, grouped error telemetry that works with APM, Sentry, and Datadog.
items.summary: samber/oops is a drop-in replacement for Go's standard error handling that adds structured context, stack traces, error codes, and user-facing messages. Developers use it at every architectural layer to ensure on-call engineers can diagnose production errors without asking developers for more information. It matters because variable data goes in attributes (not messages), allowing APM tools to group errors properly by code and reduce noise.
highlights: Structured error context with stack traces
Low-cardinality error messages for APM grouping
Domain, code, and user-facing message separation

items.name: golang-samber-mo
items.author: samber
items.description: Get precise guidance on using samber/mo Option[T] for nullable fields that must support both database scanning and JSON marshaling without extra DTOs or custom code.
items.summary: samber/mo is a Go library providing type-safe monadic types (Option, Result, Either, Future, IO, Task, State) with zero dependencies. Developers use it to replace nil checks with type constraints and transform error handling from imperative (if err != nil) to composable pipelines. It matters because impossible states become unrepresentable at the type level - Some(value) or None, Ok(value) or Err, Left(value) or Right(value) - reducing runtime crashes.
highlights: Type-safe monadic types: Option, Result, Either, Future, IO, Task, State
Eliminates nil checks and unwrap-or-panic patterns at the type level
Pipe sub-packages for composable, type-changing transformations

items.summary: Investigate-first is a Caveman debugging skill that makes agents gather proof before touching product code. It applies to intermittent failures, unknown root causes, and performance regressions where guessing leads to churn. The workflow ranks hypotheses, traces state transitions, and stops when one mechanism explains the evidence.
highlights: Forces evidence gathering before any code edits
Ranks hypotheses by cheap falsification value
Separates observed symptoms from inferred causes

items.name: golang-samber-hot
items.author: samber
items.description: Ensure Claude, Cursor or Codex correctly chooses and configures the optimal samber/hot cache algorithm and developer pattern for their specific Go workload.
items.summary: samber/hot is a generic, type-safe in-memory caching library for Go 1.22+ with 9 eviction algorithms. Developers use it to reduce latency and backend pressure when repeatedly loading the same medium-to-low cardinality resources at high frequency. It matters because the wrong algorithm (LRU when frequency dominates) tanks hit rate; W-TinyLFU is a safe default for mixed workloads.
highlights: 9 eviction algorithms (LRU, LFU, W-TinyLFU, S3FIFO, ARC, etc.)
TTL, loader chains, singleflight deduplication, stale-while-revalidate
Prometheus metrics and capacity sizing guidance

items.summary: samber/ro is a Go implementation of ReactiveX providing 150+ type-safe operators for composable asynchronous streams. Developers use it for infinite event streams (WebSocket, tickers, file watchers) where manual goroutine/channel logic becomes unwieldy. It matters because reactive streams handle backpressure, error propagation, and operator composition automatically - complex async patterns become declarative.
highlights: ReactiveX for Go: 150+ type-safe operators, cold/hot observables
Declarative pipelines replace goroutine/channel boilerplate
40+ plugins: HTTP, cron, fsnotify, Datadog, Sentry, Kafka
